source_note: MIT OpenCourseWare, 24.09 Minds and Machines (Fall 2011): Lecture Notes page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/24-09-minds-and-machines-fall-2011/pages/lecture-notes/) with the Syllabus page (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/24-09-minds-and-machines-fall-2011/pages/syllabus/); fetched 2026-10-21

lectures.title: Introduction
lectures.summary: Introduces the course and its central questions in philosophy of mind, such as whether computers can think and whether the mind is an immaterial thing or the brain.

lectures.title: Searle against artificial intelligence (AI): The Chinese room argument
lectures.summary: Presents John Searle's Chinese room argument against artificial intelligence.

lectures.title: The Chinese room argument (cont.)
lectures.summary: Continues the examination of Searle's Chinese room argument against artificial intelligence.

lectures.title: The Chinese room argument (cont.), and the Turing test
lectures.summary: Concludes the discussion of the Chinese room argument and turns to Alan Turing's test for whether computers can think.

lectures.title: The Turing test (cont.)
lectures.summary: Continues the discussion of the Turing test as a proposed test of machine intelligence.

lectures.title: Computational complexity (guest lecture by Scott Aaronson)
lectures.summary: Guest lecture by Scott Aaronson on computational complexity.

lectures.title: Dualism
lectures.summary: Begins the examination of mind–body dualism, the view that the mind is an immaterial thing.

lectures.title: Dualism (cont.)
lectures.summary: Continues the examination of mind–body dualism.

lectures.title: From dualism to behaviorism
lectures.summary: Traces the move away from dualism toward behaviorism about the mind.

lectures.title: From behaviorism to the identity theory
lectures.summary: Moves from behaviorism to the identity theory, the view that the mind is the brain.

lectures.title: The identity theory (cont.)
lectures.summary: Continues the discussion of the identity theory of the mind.

lectures.title: Kripke’s Objection
lectures.summary: Presents Saul Kripke's objection, directed in this course at the mind–brain identity theory.

lectures.title: Functionalism
lectures.summary: Introduces functionalism, on which the mind stands to the brain as a computer program stands to the hardware.

lectures.title: Review session
lectures.summary: A review session covering material from the course so far.

lectures.title: From functionalism to externalism
lectures.summary: Begins the transition from functionalism to externalism about mental content.

lectures.title: Externalism
lectures.summary: Examines externalism about mental content.

lectures.title: From externalism to perception
lectures.summary: Transitions from externalism to the philosophy of perception.

lectures.title: Perception: Valberg’s puzzle of experience
lectures.summary: Takes up Valberg's puzzle of experience in the philosophy of perception.

lectures.title: Perception, consciousness, and intentionality
lectures.summary: Explores perception, consciousness, and intentionality — the capacity to think thoughts that are about things.

lectures.title: Perception, consciousness, and intentionality (cont.)
lectures.summary: Continues the discussion of perception, consciousness, and intentionality.

lectures.title: Jackson’s knowledge argument
lectures.summary: Examines Frank Jackson's knowledge argument, a challenge to physicalism about the mind.

lectures.title: Nagel on bats
lectures.summary: Discusses Thomas Nagel's question of what it is like to be a bat and what it suggests about consciousness.

lectures.title: Consciousness and its place in nature
lectures.summary: Considers whether and how consciousness can be explained scientifically and where it fits in nature.

lectures.title: Consciousness and its place in nature (cont.)
lectures.summary: Continues the discussion of consciousness and its place in nature.

lectures.title: Free will
lectures.summary: Turns to the problem of free will versus determinism.

lectures.title: Last lecture, including information about the final exam
lectures.summary: The final lecture of the course, which also includes information about the final exam.
